# Draft:World Heritage and Recognition of Bengal

World Heritage and Recognition of Bengal, or World Heritage and Recognition of the Bengal region, refers to the architectural structures, archaeological sites, cultural practices, documentary heritage, and other forms of recognition found across the entire Bengal delta region, including present-day Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal, that have been recognized by UNESCO or other international convention as World Heritage or under other important international designations. At present, there are a total of 16 World Heritage and recognized elements in this region. These include 6 World Heritage Sites, 7 elements of Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2 inscriptions in the Memory of the World Register, and 1 internationally recognized observance day.
Among the World Heritage Sites, those located in Bangladesh include the Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat, the Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur, and the Sundarbans. In West Bengal, the listed sites include Sundarbans National Park, the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway under the title Mountain Railways of India, and Shantiniketan. The elements inscribed as Intangible Cultural Heritage include Baul songs of Bangladesh, the traditional art of Jamdani weaving, the Mangal Shobhajatra held in Dhaka during Pohela Boishakh, the traditional Shital Pati weaving of Sylhet, and rickshaws and rickshaw painting of Dhaka. Most recently, the traditional saree weaving of Tangail in Bangladesh has also been recognized as part of this cultural heritage. From West Bengal, Durga Puja in Kolkata has been included in the list. Under documentary heritage, the historic 7 March Speech of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and the novella Sultana’s Dream written by Begum Rokeya have been recognized in the Memory of the World Register. In addition, 21 February has been internationally recognized as International Mother Language Day.
At present, among the total 16 World Heritage and recognized elements of Bengal, 12 are located in Bangladesh and 4 are under West Bengal. In UNESCO’s Tentative Lists, 7 sites from Bangladesh and 2 sites from West Bengal have been placed under consideration for future World Heritage nomination. In addition, the region also includes 4 Ramsar sites.

At present, the Bengal region has a total of six UNESCO-recognized World Heritage Sites. These include the Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat, the Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur, the Sundarbans in Bangladesh, which is the world’s largest mangrove forest, Sundarbans National Park in West Bengal, the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, and Santiniketan. UNESCO inscribed the Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat and the Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur in 1985, Sundarbans National Park in West Bengal in 1987, the Sundarbans of Bangladesh in 1997, the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway in 1999, and most recently Santiniketan in 2023 as World Heritage Sites.
Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat
]]
The Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat is a medieval urban center located in southwestern Bangladesh, on the outskirts of present-day Bagerhat District, near the confluence of the Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems. The city was formerly known as Khalifatabad and was established in the fifteenth century by the Turkic-origin ruler and military commander Ulugh Khan Jahan. Within a relatively short period during his rule, the city developed in a planned manner and emerged as an important Islamic administrative and religious center in southwestern Bengal. The city extended over an area of approximately 50 square kilometres and preserves remarkable examples of early Islamic architecture in the region. At its height, around 360 mosques, along with numerous mausoleums, bridges, roads, reservoirs, and public utility structures, were constructed in the city, most of them built of baked brick. Following the death of Ulugh Khan Jahan in 1459, the city gradually declined and was eventually abandoned, later becoming covered by the forests of the Sundarbans.
One notable feature of the city is the absence of defensive walls, suggesting that the difficult wetlands of the Sundarbans served as a natural form of protection. The urban layout also demonstrates advanced water management systems and considerable engineering skill in the construction of roads and bridges. Architecturally, the site represents a distinctive style known as the Khan Jahan style, which holds a unique place in the architectural history of Bengal. Among its monuments, the Sixty Dome Mosque is particularly significant and is considered unparalleled in Bengal in terms of both scale and design.
Under cultural criterion (iv), the entire city of Bagerhat, including the Sixty Dome Mosque, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site under the title Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat (Bengali: Mosque City of Bagerhat) at the 9th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, held in Paris, France, from 2 to 6 December 1985. The site is currently preserved under the supervision of the Department of Archaeology of Bangladesh, and conservation activities are ongoing to maintain its historical integrity and authenticity.
Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur
The ruins of Somapura Mahavihara, also known as the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur, located in Paharpur of Naogaon District, are regarded as one of the most significant and remarkable archaeological sites of the pre-Islamic period in Bangladesh. The monastery represents clear evidence of the development of Mahayana Buddhism in Bengal from around the seventh century CE. It was constructed by the Pala dynasty ruler Dharmapala (c. 770–810 CE), a fact confirmed by an inscribed clay seal discovered within the monastery complex. Somapura Mahavihara was not only a religious institution but also developed into a renowned international centre of learning and Buddhist scholarship until the twelfth century, where Vajrayana-oriented Mahayana Buddhist practices flourished and numerous Buddhist texts were composed.
Architecturally, the complex was built on a vast quadrangular plan measuring approximately 920 feet in length. At its centre stands a cruciform main temple surrounded by a residential monastery containing a total of 177 monastic cells. The central terraced structure, rising in three successive levels, reaches a height of about 70 feet. Its decorative terracotta plaques and carved ornamental features significantly influenced Buddhist architectural traditions across South and Southeast Asia. The impact of this architectural style extended particularly to Pagan in present-day Myanmar, central Java in Indonesia, and regions as far as Cambodia, establishing its outstanding universal value under UNESCO cultural criteria (i) and (ii). The site is also recognized as the second-largest single Buddhist monastery south of the Himalayas.
Although the principal structural remains of the monument are still preserved, parts of the terracotta plaques and brick masonry are currently threatened by environmental weathering, salinity, and vegetation growth. The site is legally protected and maintained under the supervision of the Department of Archaeology of Bangladesh; however, UNESCO has emphasized the need for strengthened buffer zones and modern conservation policies to ensure its long-term preservation.
Owing to its historical and religious significance, Somapura Mahavihara was inscribed as a World Heritage Site under the title Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur (Bengali: Paharpur Buddhist Vihara) during the 9th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee held in Paris, France, from 2 to 6 December 1985, on the basis of cultural criteria (i), (ii), and (vi) (Dossier No. 322).
Sundarbans
The Sundarbans is the largest contiguous mangrove forest in the world, located in the delta formed by the Padma, Brahmaputra, and Meghna river systems along the coast of the Bay of Bengal. The forest covers an area of approximately 10,000 square kilometres, of which about 66 percent lies within Bangladesh and the remaining portion within India. In the Bangladeshi part, the forest includes roughly 414,259 hectares of land, including newly formed islands and mudflats, along with about 187,413 hectares of waterways. The region consists of a complex network of tidal rivers, creeks, mudflats, and salt-tolerant mangrove islands, representing a living example of an active deltaic ecosystem.
The reserved forest of the Sundarbans in Bangladesh extends across the southwestern region from the Baleshwar River to the Harinbhanga River and remains directly connected to the Bay of Bengal. The area forms a distinct ecological and climatic zone and has long been associated with mythology, folklore, and historical traditions. Owing to its natural beauty and ecological resources, the Sundarbans is internationally recognized for its exceptional biodiversity. The forest supports approximately 334 species of plants, 165 species of algae, and 13 species of orchids. Its fauna includes around 693 species of wildlife, comprising mammals, reptiles, amphibians, fish, shrimp, crabs, and molluscs. The Sundarbans also serves as an important habitat for about 315 species of birds. The forest is closely linked to the livelihoods and security of millions of people living in surrounding coastal areas, acting as a natural barrier against cyclones, storm surges, and saline water intrusion. Despite challenges posed by climate change, increasing salinity, cyclones, illegal hunting, and overexploitation of forest resources, its ecological significance and outstanding universal value remain intact. The Sundarbans provides a critical refuge for many globally threatened species, including the Royal Bengal Tiger, the Ganges and Irrawaddy dolphins, estuarine crocodiles, and the critically endangered northern river terrapin (Batagur baska). Notably, it is the only natural mangrove habitat in the world supporting a population of Royal Bengal Tigers. Various surveys estimate that the forest supports approximately 400 to 450 Royal Bengal Tigers, representing one of the highest population densities of the species worldwide. The World Heritage property within Bangladesh covers about 139,500 hectares and includes three wildlife sanctuaries that function as key breeding grounds for numerous endangered species.
Historically, the Sundarbans was declared a reserved forest in 1878, and three wildlife sanctuaries were established in 1977. Activities such as entry, hunting, fishing, and extraction of forest resources are regulated under the Forest Act of 1927 and the Bangladesh Wildlife (Preservation) Act of 1974. At present, the forest is managed through regular monitoring and scientific conservation practices aimed at protecting biodiversity, scenic value, and ecological integrity.
The Sundarbans was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List under the title The Sundarbans during the 21st session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee held in Paris, France, in December 1997. It was listed as a natural World Heritage Site under criteria (ix) and (x), recognizing its outstanding ecological processes and exceptional biodiversity conservation value. Although the Sundarbans of Bangladesh and the Sundarbans National Park of India form parts of the same continuous forest ecosystem, UNESCO has listed them separately as The Sundarbans (Bangladesh) and Sundarbans National Park (India). Earlier, on 21 May 1992, the Sundarbans was also designated as a Ramsar site.
Sundarbans National Park
Sundarbans National Park forms part of the world’s largest mangrove forest located in the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta region, covering a total area of approximately 10,000 square kilometres across both land and water. About 66 percent of this ecosystem lies in Bangladesh, while the remaining portion is situated in India. The region is internationally recognized as one of the most biologically diverse natural ecosystems in the world. It supports around 78 species of mangrove plants, making it one of the most diverse mangrove forests globally. The Sundarbans is especially renowned for the Royal Bengal Tiger, which represents the largest single population of tigers in the world adapted to a tidal mangrove environment and capable of a semi-aquatic lifestyle. The area is also an important habitat for the Irrawaddy and Ganges river dolphins, the king cobra, endangered river terrapins, and serves as a breeding ground for marine turtles such as the olive ridley, green, and hawksbill turtles.
Ecologically, the Sundarbans functions as an effective natural barrier against cyclones, protecting coastal regions from severe natural disasters. It also plays a crucial role in sediment retention, coastal stabilization, and serving as a nursery ground for numerous marine species. Continuous tidal action causes both erosion and sediment deposition, leading to the constant formation of new islands and waterways, making the area an outstanding example of active deltaic processes. Sundarbans National Park covers an area of approximately 133,010 hectares, of which about 55 percent consists of forested land and 45 percent comprises rivers, creeks, estuaries, and wetlands. The park forms part of the larger UNESCO-designated Biosphere Reserve declared in November 2001, while surrounding sanctuaries provide additional buffer protection. However, reduced upstream freshwater flow in the Ganges during the dry season, changing salinity levels, oil pollution, and human–tiger conflict have been identified as major conservation challenges.
Legally, Sundarbans National Park is protected under the Indian Forest Act of 1927, the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972, and the Environment Protection Act of 1986. Conservation activities are carried out under an approved management plan, although UNESCO has emphasized the need to strengthen long-term protection through enhanced research, monitoring, alternative livelihood opportunities for local communities, and participatory management approaches.
Sundarbans National Park, located in the Indian state of West Bengal, was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List under natural criteria (ix) and (x) during the 11th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee held in Paris, France, in 1987, under the title Sundarbans National Park (Bengali: Sundarbans National Park).
Darjeeling Himalayan Railway (under the title Mountain Railways of India)
The UNESCO World Heritage property Mountain Railways of India comprises three historic mountain railway systems in India, among which the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway is the oldest and the most internationally recognized example. These railways were constructed under British colonial administration between the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries (1881–1908) and demonstrate remarkable engineering achievements in establishing effective rail communication across difficult and scenic mountainous terrain.
At the centre of this heritage property is the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, which began operation in 1881 and remains functional to this day. The railway extends approximately 88.5 kilometres with a narrow gauge of 2 feet (0.610 metres), running from New Jalpaiguri to Darjeeling and reaching an elevation of about 2,258 metres at Ghum station, one of the highest railway stations in India. To overcome steep mountain gradients, the railway employs innovative engineering solutions such as zigzag reverses and loop systems, making it one of the most distinctive mountain railways in the world. Beyond serving as a transportation system, the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway represents a living example of colonial-era technology, the development of hill settlements, and historical patterns of life in the Himalayan region. Owing to its antiquity, innovative design, and cultural significance, it holds a central symbolic importance within this World Heritage property.
The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway was inscribed as a World Heritage Site under the title Mountain Railways of India during the 23rd session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee held in Marrakesh, Morocco, on 5 December 1999. Subsequently, two additional railway systems were included under the same designation: the Nilgiri Mountain Railway in 2005 and the Kalka–Shimla Railway in 2008.
Santiniketan
Santiniketan was established in 1901 in the rural region of present-day West Bengal, India, through the initiative of the poet and philosopher Rabindranath Tagore. It began as a residential school and a centre for artistic and intellectual practice, where ancient Indian educational traditions, a close relationship with nature, and the philosophy of human unity beyond religious and cultural divisions were brought together. This vision later led to the establishment of Visva-Bharati in 1921 as a universal university intended to promote the idea of the unity of humanity. Distinct from the dominant trends of British colonial architecture and European modernism in the early twentieth century, Santiniketan reflected a form of pan-Asian modernity. The institution incorporated elements drawn from ancient, medieval, and folk traditions alongside artistic influences from India, Japan, China, Persia, Bali, and other parts of Asia. Open-air classrooms beneath trees, combined with artistic practice, music, and nature-based learning, embodied Tagore’s educational philosophy of creating a place where the world could meet within a shared cultural home.
Santiniketan was not merely an educational institution but also an experimental community where artists, thinkers, teachers, and craftspeople lived and worked together. This environment significantly influenced educational thought, artistic development, literature, and cultural movements across South Asia. The Ashram area, Uttarayan complex, and Kala Bhavana precinct together illustrate a unique integration of education, art, architecture, and the natural landscape. For these reasons, Santiniketan is regarded as an exceptional example of an experimental model of education and community life. It is valued both as a distinctive humanistic educational environment and as a site directly and livingly associated with the ideals of Rabindranath Tagore. Today, the heritage property consists of a core area of approximately 36 hectares and a buffer zone of about 537.73 hectares. The site remains active as part of Visva-Bharati University and continues to sustain its educational and cultural traditions.
Santiniketan was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List under the title Santiniketan during the extended 45th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee held in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on 17 September 2023. It was recognized under cultural criteria (iv) and (vi).
